claims_checked.claim: The image is a real, published VB data-entry UI with a named creator and source.
claims_checked.notes: Microsoft Corporation, December 1998 article, Figure 16. File fetched anonymously from the Microsoft Learn archive; SHA-256 recorded.

claims_checked.claim: Public availability means the image may be used.

Microsoft's copyrighted-content guidelines are a possible permission route, with conditions (attribution statement, resize only, no portions, no third-party content). Whether they cover a documentation figure used in a video and a collage is a legal/policy judgement that evidence cannot settle.

gates.title: Popularity, installed base, prices, and real VB applications

claims_checked.claim: The pictured data-entry form was built with Visual Basic (implementation language, not just appearance).
claims_checked.notes: Microsoft's own article says the Data Object Wizard is a Visual Basic 6.0 add-in that generates Visual Basic User Controls, and captions this figure as a DOW-generated Single Record User Control. The field names match the article's sample stored procedures.

claims_checked.claim: The asset shows a real-world VB application of the kind the narration describes (accountants, teachers, small business owners).
claims_checked.notes: It is Microsoft's documentation example of wizard-generated VB UI, with sample data, not a tool written by an end user. It is a documented VB data-entry form. It does not prove the narration's claims about who wrote VB software. No statistics or rankings appear in the artwork.

claims_checked.claim: Era matches the script's mid-1990s framing.
claims_checked.notes: Classic VB (VB6, December 1998), not VB3/VB4. Borrow-only Internet Archive scans of the VB3 Data Access Guide exist but could not be accessed without an account.

gates.reason: No statistics appear in artwork. Collage applications have documented VB provenance; the narration's generalisations are illustrative colour by producer decision. A Microsoft VB6 documentation figure is acceptable as the data-entry panel; no on-screen note needed, the credit identifies it.
gates.approver: Producer (vb-video-checkout-2-38, Claude Fable 5.1), under Devin's 2026-09-15 delegation of release review
gates.decision: Approved: the asset matches the script and source as they now stand.

review_questions.question: Can this Microsoft documentation figure (VB6 Data Object Wizard article, Figure 16, December 1998) be used in the video and in the XTRA-14/15 collage under Microsoft's "Use of Microsoft copyrighted content" screenshot guidelines, with the credit "Used with permission from Microsoft"? Those guidelines allow resizing only and forbid portions of screenshots, so a collage that crops, overlaps or rotates it may not qualify. If not, should the project request written permission or drop the image?
review_questions.blocks: release only; production proof is usable by dependents

resolution.decision: A Microsoft VB6 documentation figure is acceptable as the data-entry panel; no on-screen note needed, the credit identifies it.

review_questions.question: The best-provenanced data-entry form found is a Microsoft sample (wizard-generated VB6 control with dummy data), not an application built by an accountant, teacher or small-business owner. Is a documented Microsoft VB sample acceptable in a collage the script describes as real-world VB applications, and should an on-screen or edit note identify it as a Microsoft VB6 documentation example? No SCRIPT.md change is proposed.

resolution.decision: A Microsoft VB6 documentation figure is acceptable as the data-entry panel; no on-screen note needed, the credit identifies it.

review_questions.question: The script's framing is mid-1990s VB ($100 purchase, library book), but this figure is VB6 from late 1998. Is a 1998 classic-VB image acceptable, or should the project seek a VB3/VB4-era data form? The known VB3 Data Access Guide scan on Internet Archive is borrow-only, so getting it would need a human with an account (a boundary action).

resolution.decision: A Microsoft VB6 documentation figure is acceptable as the data-entry panel; no on-screen note needed, the credit identifies it.
